grid.title: Grid: clean lines
steps: Stand where you will practice, with both staves in view. Press Auto-fit, then spin normally for two seconds; it centers and sizes the grid once. Reset guide layout restores the default.
The lime line is staff A and the purple line is staff B, drawn between each staff's two tracked ends. The colors only tell the staves apart. Faint curves show each tip's path over the last 4 seconds.
An amber ring and arrow mark a tip that is off the grid: move that tip into the white TARGET ring on the nearest line. A white ring with a check means that tip is within tolerance.

Size sets the grid width; Match staff length sets it to one staff length. If another light is tracked, choose your LED colors or capture the background. For an off-angle camera, use Calibrate viewing angle.

circles.title: Circles: steady radii
steps: Get into your spinning position with both staves in view. Press Auto-fit and spin normally for two seconds; it estimates circle size, center and separation. Reset guide layout restores the default.
Trace the white circles with your tips. An amber ring and arrow show which way to move a tip into its white TARGET ring on the circle. A white ring with a check means that tip is within tolerance.
Match staff length sets each circle's diameter to your staff length. Circle separation spreads the circles apart. One-staff mode uses a single circle.

Beat practice follows the end labeled BEAT TIP. Pass it across a numbered point on each blue pulse. With 4 points at 120 BPM, one full circle takes 2 seconds. Timing and position are scored separately. Open How beat practice works for the full explanation.

cube.title: Cube: align with vertices
steps: The cube is a flat drawing, not measured depth. Press Auto-fit with your staves in view, then adjust Size and Cube projection depth so the corners sit where you want to reach.
Aim tips at the white corner points. An amber ring and arrow lead from a tip to its nearest corner, marked by a white TARGET ring. A white ring with a check means that tip is on a corner.
If the camera is off to one side, use Calibrate viewing angle on a real rectangle in your movement plane. It corrects that plane only, not movement toward or away from the camera.
Use cube error for chosen alignment moments; moves between corners naturally score worse. The lime and purple lines only identify staff A and staff B.

free.title: Free flow: watch your paths
steps: Keep your whole movement in view. Free flow has no alignment score, so no arrows or targets appear.
The lime line is staff A and the purple line is staff B, drawn between each staff's tracked ends. Faint curves show where each tip went in the last 4 seconds; gaps mean the tip was hidden or unclear.
Identical staves can swap after being fully hidden; use Identify staves to correct them. If a lamp or window is tracked, choose your LED colors or capture the background.
Beat practice still works here: numbered points sit on a circle around the guide center. Auto-fit or Size changes that circle. Record a session to review your paths later.

antispin.title: Linear antispin: one tip on each line
steps: Use one double-ended staff. Trace the horizontal line with one tip (H TIP), and the vertical line with the other (V TIP). The shaft rotates freely between them. This mode selects one staff automatically.

Place the cross where your two tip paths intersect. Set Rotation to 0 for level horizontal/vertical lines. Match staff length sets center-to-edge distance to one full staff length, so the whole cross is two staff lengths wide. Step back if it will not fit.

Get ready, then press Auto-fit and complete a full antispin cycle during its two-second sample. Check Center X/Y afterward. For an off-angle camera, calibrate a rectangle in your movement plane first. Amber arrows lead from each tip to its assigned line; checked rings mean within tolerance.

The alignment box shows separate horizontal/vertical drift averaged over five seconds. Tolerance is a percent of the full cross width. For beats, alternate tips at the four outer turnarounds, one per pulse; 120 BPM gives a two-second cycle. Open How beat practice works for details.
